title: When Two Go Together
text:
In Book 10 of Homer's Iliad, the Greeks were in a desperate situation. The Trojans were camped on the plain right next to the Greek ships, their fires burning in the dark, and the Greek leaders could not sleep. Old Nestor asked whether anyone would dare to slip into the Trojan camp at night and find out what the enemy planned.

Diomedes, one of the bravest of the Greeks, volunteered at once. But he said he wanted a companion. When two go together, he explained, one may notice an opportunity before the other, while a man alone thinks less quickly and his judgment is thinner. Many offered to go with him, and he was told to choose whomever he liked. He chose Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, because he was resourceful and the goddess Athena favored him.

The two set out into the darkness. They caught a Trojan scout named Dolon, who was on his way to spy on the Greek ships, and made him tell them where the enemy's newly arrived allies were camped. They found the Thracian king Rhesus asleep with his men. Diomedes did the killing, while Odysseus pulled the bodies aside so the horses would not shy at them. Then they drove the king's famous white horses back to the Greek camp.
lesson: For a hard job, pick a partner who sees what you miss. Two people with complementary strengths notice more and recover faster than one person alone.
location: Ancient Greece (story set at Troy, modern Turkey)
caveat: Many scholars think Book 10 was added to the Iliad later than the rest of the poem.
